prompt: On a road with two or more lanes going your way, which lane is mainly meant for passing?
choices: The far-right lane
The paved shoulder
The far-left lane
Any lane, since they are all the same
explanation: The left lane is the passing lane. Slower traffic should keep to the right and use the left lane to pass, then move back.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., TX p. 37, NJ p. 67, AZ p. 32-33)

prompt: You are driving slower than most of the traffic on a multilane road. Which lane should you use?
choices: The right lane
The left lane
The center left-turn lane
Whichever lane has the fewest cars
explanation: Slower traffic keeps right so faster drivers can pass on the left. Cruising slowly in the left lane forces others to weave around you.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., TX p. 37, NJ p. 67, AZ p. 32-33)

prompt: When you overtake a vehicle going the same direction as you, on which side do you normally pass?
choices: On the right
On whichever side has more room
On either side, as long as you signal
On the left
explanation: Passing is normally done on the left. Passing on the right is allowed only in limited situations and only when it is safe.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., CA p. 31, AZ p. 27, NY p. 39)

prompt: You plan to change lanes to the left. Which way should you turn your head to check your blind spot?
choices: Over your right shoulder
Over your left shoulder
Straight back through the rear window
You don't need to if your mirrors are set
explanation: Look quickly over the shoulder on the side you are moving toward. That is where a car hidden from your mirrors could be.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., CA p. 21, NE p. 63, NJ p. 98)

prompt: What is a blind spot?
choices: The area your headlights do not light up at night
An area around your vehicle that you cannot see in your mirrors
A place where sun glare blinds you
The space between your car and the car ahead
explanation: Blind spots are areas beside and behind your car that your mirrors do not show. You must turn your head to check them.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., AZ p. 26, NY p. 39, NJ p. 98)

prompt: Where are the blind spots on a typical car?
choices: Only directly in front of the hood
Only on the passenger side
Only directly behind the rear bumper
Beside and slightly behind the car, on both the left and right sides
explanation: Even well-adjusted mirrors leave blind spots behind both sides of the car. A vehicle there may not show up in any mirror.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., AZ p. 26, NY p. 39, NJ p. 98)

prompt: Another vehicle is passing you on the left. What should you do?
choices: Stay in your lane and do not speed up
Speed up so the driver can't cut in front of you
Move toward the center line
Brake hard to a stop
explanation: Make the pass easy: keep your lane and never speed up. Speeding up can trap the passing driver in the other lane.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., TX p. 45, AZ p. 27, NH p. 23)

prompt: Why is it dangerous to start passing as you approach the top of a hill?
choices: Your car loses too much power going uphill
The driver ahead is required to speed up
You cannot see oncoming traffic on the other side
Your mirrors don't work on a slope
explanation: A hill crest blocks your view of oncoming vehicles. Never pass when you cannot see far enough ahead to be sure it is safe.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., AZ p. 28, PA p. 51, TX p. 44, NJ p. 67)

prompt: On a two-lane road, there is a solid yellow line on your side of the center line. What does it mean?
choices: You may pass if it looks safe
You may pass only in daylight
You may not pass
The lane is for left turns only
explanation: A solid yellow line on your side marks a no-passing zone. A broken line on your side means passing is allowed when safe.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., PA p. 26, NJ p. 66, CA p. 19)

prompt: Should you signal a lane change even if you don't see any other vehicles nearby?
choices: Yes, always signal before changing lanes
No, only when cars are close behind you
Only on highways
Only at night
explanation: Signal every lane change. The vehicle you don't see, such as one in your blind spot, is the most dangerous one.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., AZ p. 26, NY p. 39, NJ p. 98)

prompt: A lane is marked on both sides by double broken (dashed) yellow lines. What kind of lane is it most likely?
choices: A two-way left-turn lane
A bicycle lane
A lane for emergency vehicles only
A reversible lane whose direction changes at certain times
explanation: Reversible lanes are usually marked with double dashed yellow lines. Check signs or overhead signals to see which way the lane is open.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., AZ p. 46, NM p. 12, AK p. 58, AL p. 58)

prompt: An overhead lane signal shows a red X above your lane. What does it mean?
choices: The lane is open, but drive with caution
Do not drive in that lane
The lane is for left turns only
Stop, then continue in the lane
explanation: A red X means the lane is closed to you, often because opposing traffic is using it. Move to a lane with a green arrow.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., AZ p. 46, NM p. 12, AK p. 58, AL p. 58)

prompt: An overhead lane signal shows a green downward arrow above your lane. What does it mean?
choices: You must turn at the next intersection
You may drive in that lane
The lane is about to close
Only buses may use the lane
explanation: A green arrow pointing down means you are permitted to travel in the lane below it, while still obeying all other signs and signals.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., AZ p. 46, NM p. 12, AK p. 58, AL p. 58)

prompt: What is an HOV (high-occupancy vehicle) lane for?
choices: Large trucks and buses only
Drivers who want to go faster than the speed limit
Stopping in an emergency
Vehicles carrying at least the minimum number of people shown on the signs
explanation: HOV lanes are reserved for vehicles with a posted minimum number of occupants (and others the signs allow) during posted times.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., CA p. 21-22, AZ p. 33, NM p. 12)

prompt: May you use a shared center left-turn lane to pass a slow vehicle?
choices: No, it is reserved for turning, not passing
Yes, if you signal first
Yes, if no one is turning
Yes, but only at night
explanation: A two-way center left-turn lane is used to prepare for and make left turns (and U-turns where allowed). It is not a travel lane or a passing lane.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., CA p. 22, PA p. 49)

prompt: Your lane is ending ahead. What should you do?
choices: Stop at the end of your lane and wait
Speed up and force your way in
Signal, adjust your speed, and merge into a safe gap
Drive on the shoulder until a gap opens
explanation: Watch for lane-ends signs and markings, signal early, match the flow of traffic, and merge smoothly when there is room.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., CO p. 22, CA p. 20, PA p. 50)

prompt: Why should you avoid weaving in and out of lanes?
choices: It wears out your turn signals
It is only a problem on freeways
Frequent lane changes greatly increase the chance of a crash
It slows you down too much
explanation: Stay in one lane as much as possible. Each lane change is a chance for a conflict with another vehicle.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., CA p. 21, NE p. 63, NJ p. 98)

prompt: On a two-lane, two-way road, where should you drive when you are not passing?
choices: On the right side of the road
Straddling the center line
In the middle of the road
On the left side if it is smoother
explanation: Drivers must keep to the right half of the road except when passing or when the right side is blocked.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., TX p. 37, NJ p. 67, AZ p. 32-33)

prompt: Which order is best for a safe lane change?
choices: Move over, then signal, then check your mirrors
Check mirrors, change lanes, then signal
Signal and move over at the same moment
Signal, check mirrors, look over your shoulder, then move over gradually
explanation: Signal first so others know your plan, check mirrors and your blind spot, make sure there is room, then move smoothly into the lane.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., CA p. 21, NE p. 63, NJ p. 98)

prompt: You are on a multilane street and need to get from the right lane to the far-left lane for a turn ahead. How should you do it?
choices: Cross all the lanes in one smooth move
Change one lane at a time, signaling and checking each time
Wait until the intersection and cut over
Straddle the lane lines until traffic clears
explanation: Move one lane at a time, signaling and checking mirrors and blind spots before each move. Plan ahead so you are not rushed.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., CA p. 21, NE p. 63, NJ p. 98)

prompt: On a two-lane road, the center line is solid on the far side and broken on your side. A slow car is ahead and the road is clear. What may you do?
choices: You may not pass at all
Pass when it is safe, because the broken line is on your side
Pass only if the oncoming lane has a broken line
Pass only if the slow driver waves you on
explanation: You may pass when the broken line is on your side and it is safe. Drivers on the side with the solid line may not pass.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., PA p. 26, NJ p. 66, CA p. 19)

prompt: A two-lane road has double solid yellow center lines. What does this mean for drivers who want to pass a car ahead?
choices: Passing is allowed if the road ahead looks clear
Passing is allowed only in daylight
Passing is allowed if you sound your horn first
Passing is not allowed from either direction
explanation: Double solid yellow lines prohibit passing in both directions, even if no NO PASSING sign is posted.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., PA p. 26, NJ p. 66, CA p. 19)

prompt: You are passing on a two-lane road and see that a no-passing zone begins just ahead. What must you do?
choices: Finish the pass and be back in your lane before the no-passing zone begins
Keep passing, since you started in a legal zone
Turn on your hazard lights and continue
Slow down and stay beside the other car
explanation: All passing must be completed before the solid line on your side begins. If you can't make it, don't start the pass.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., AZ p. 28, PA p. 51, TX p. 44, NJ p. 67)

prompt: On a two-lane road, the car ahead slows and signals a left turn. What should you do?
choices: Pass on the left quickly before it turns
Pass on the left if no oncoming cars are coming
Do not pass on the left; slow down and wait, or pass on the right only if there is room and it is safe
Sound your horn so the driver hurries
explanation: Never pass on the left of a driver who is signaling a left turn. Passing on the right is allowed only when there is enough room and it is safe.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., CA p. 31, NY p. 39-40, NJ p. 67, AZ p. 27)

prompt: When is passing on the right generally allowed?
choices: Whenever the left lane is busy
Whenever the driver ahead is below the speed limit
When there are two or more lanes going your direction and it can be done safely
Never, under any circumstances
explanation: Passing on the right is allowed in limited cases, such as a multilane road in your direction or a car ahead turning left, and only when safe.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., CA p. 31, NY p. 39-40, NJ p. 67, AZ p. 27)

prompt: You are on a one-way street with two lanes. A slow vehicle is in the left lane. May you pass it on the right?
choices: Yes, if it is safe
No, you must always pass on the left
Only if the driver signals you
Only if you use the shoulder
explanation: On a one-way street with two or more lanes, you may pass on either side when it is safe to do so.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., CA p. 31, NY p. 39-40, NJ p. 67, AZ p. 27)

prompt: Your car has a blind-spot monitor and its warning light is off. You want to change lanes. What should you still do?
choices: Nothing; the monitor has already checked
Rely on your mirrors only
Just signal and move over
Look over your shoulder to check the blind spot
explanation: Blind-spot monitors and backup cameras are aids, not replacements for a visual check of your mirrors and blind spots.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., AZ p. 26, NY p. 39, NJ p. 98)

prompt: On a multilane highway, you have been driving right next to another car's rear corner for a while. What should you do?
choices: Stay there and match the car's speed
Speed up or drop back so the other driver can see you
Tap your horn every few seconds
Move closer to the lane line so you are noticed
explanation: Don't linger in another driver's blind spot. Either pass them or drop back so you are visible.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., AZ p. 26, NY p. 39, NJ p. 98)

prompt: You are in the left lane of a multilane highway and a faster driver comes up behind you. What should you do?
choices: Stay in the left lane to keep the driver at the speed limit
Move to the right when it is safe and let the driver pass
Tap your brakes to warn the driver
Speed up to match the driver
explanation: Let faster traffic pass. Move right when safe; blocking or brake-checking a following driver invites a crash.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., TX p. 37, NJ p. 67, AZ p. 32-33)

prompt: You are being passed on a two-lane road that has no lane markings. What helps the other driver pass safely?
choices: Move toward the center of the road
Speed up so the pass ends sooner
Stop completely in the roadway
Keep to the right as far as is safe and don't speed up
explanation: When being passed, stay right and keep your speed steady or ease off slightly. Make the pass as safe and easy as possible.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., TX p. 45, AZ p. 27, NH p. 23)

prompt: You are in the left lane of a multilane road and many vehicles keep passing you on the right. What should you do?
choices: Move into the right lane and let them pass on the left
Stay in the left lane, since you are under the limit
Speed up to match the fastest car
Turn on your hazard lights
explanation: If traffic is passing you on the right, you are likely holding up the left lane. Move right so others can pass on the left.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., TX p. 45, AZ p. 27, NH p. 23)

prompt: The car in the lane next to you has stopped at a crosswalk. Your lane is clear. What should you do?
choices: Pass it carefully, since your lane is clear
Sound your horn and pass
Slow down and do not pass it; a pedestrian may be crossing
Change into its lane behind it and wait
explanation: Never pass a vehicle stopped at a crosswalk. It may be stopped for a pedestrian you cannot see.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., CA p. 47, NY p. 39, AK p. 48, NE p. 77)

prompt: Why should you watch for driveways and side roads before you pass?
choices: Passing is only allowed next to driveways
Driveways mean the speed limit goes up
A vehicle could pull out into the lane you are using to pass
Side roads always have no-passing signs
explanation: Drivers entering the road may turn into the lane you are using and may not look your way. Avoid passing near places where vehicles enter or cross.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., MT p. 77, PA p. 51)

prompt: Why is passing on a two-lane road at night especially risky?
choices: It is harder to judge how far away and how fast oncoming headlights are
Other drivers must use high beams at night
Passing at night is illegal everywhere
Your mirrors are less accurate at night
explanation: At night you can't see as far ahead, and an oncoming car may be closer than its headlights make it seem.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., MT p. 77, PA p. 51)

prompt: You are behind a slow truck on a two-lane road and a railroad crossing is just ahead. What should you do?
choices: Pass quickly before the crossing
Pass only if the crossing gates are up
Pass on the right shoulder
Stay behind the truck until well past the crossing
explanation: Do not pass at or near railroad crossings, intersections, bridges or tunnels. The vehicle you pass can block your view of hazards.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., AZ p. 28, PA p. 51, TX p. 44, NJ p. 67)

prompt: Why should you avoid passing on or near a narrow bridge, tunnel, or underpass?
choices: Bridges are always one-way
There is little room and your view of oncoming traffic may be blocked
Tunnels have lower speed limits
Your tires may lose grip on the bridge joints
explanation: Narrow bridges and tunnels leave no room to escape and often limit your view ahead. Wait until you are past them.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., AZ p. 28, PA p. 51, TX p. 44, NJ p. 67)

prompt: After passing a car, how do you know you are far enough ahead to return to your lane?
choices: As soon as your front bumper is past its front bumper
You can see both of its headlights in your inside rearview mirror
When the other driver flashes the headlights
When you have passed its back bumper
explanation: Wait until you can see the front of the passed vehicle (both headlights) in your rearview mirror, signal, check, then move back.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., PA p. 51, MT p. 77, TX p. 45, AZ p. 27)

prompt: Why shouldn't you cut back into your lane too soon after passing?
choices: You will lose your place in traffic
Your turn signal will not cancel
It wastes fuel
The driver you passed may have to brake suddenly or could hit you
explanation: Returning too soon cuts off the other driver. Leave enough room and signal before moving back.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., PA p. 51, MT p. 77, TX p. 45, AZ p. 27)

prompt: You just finished changing lanes. What should you check?
choices: That your turn signal has turned off
That your hazard lights are on
That your high beams are on
That your parking brake is released
explanation: A signal left on after a lane change tells other drivers you are about to turn or move again. Cancel it once you are done.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., CA p. 21, NE p. 63, NJ p. 98)

prompt: You are about to enter a lane marked with double dashed yellow lines. What should you check first?
choices: Nothing; these lanes always carry traffic going your way
Whether any trucks are using it
The signs or overhead signals showing which direction the lane is open to at that time
Whether your headlights are on high beam
explanation: The direction of a reversible lane changes by time of day. Read the posted signs or lane signals before you drive in it.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., AZ p. 46, NM p. 12, AK p. 58, AL p. 58)

prompt: A sign above an HOV lane reads "HOV 2+." What does it mean?
choices: At least two passengers plus the driver are required
Only two-axle vehicles may use the lane
At least two people, counting the driver, must be in the vehicle
The lane is HOV-only for two hours
explanation: The number is the minimum number of occupants, and the driver counts. Signs also show the hours and days the rule applies.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., CA p. 21-22, AZ p. 33, NM p. 12)

prompt: Where can you find out how many people are required and what hours an HOV lane's rules apply?
choices: On the signs posted along the road and at the lane entrances
The rules are the same on every highway in the country
Only on your vehicle registration
There are no set rules; any car may use it
explanation: HOV requirements vary by road and time. Signs show the minimum number of people and the hours the restriction is in effect.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., CA p. 21-22, AZ p. 33, NM p. 12)

prompt: What is a "zipper merge"?
choices: All drivers move into the open lane as soon as they see the first sign
Drivers in the ending lane must stop and wait for a gap
Drivers swap lanes back and forth to keep speed up
Drivers in two lanes take turns moving into the remaining lane where the lanes come together
explanation: In a zipper merge, both lanes are used up to the merge point, and then vehicles alternate into the open lane, one from each side.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., CO p. 22, CA p. 20, PA p. 50)

prompt: You are in a through lane, and a driver in the lane next to you is trying to merge because their lane ends. What should you do?
choices: Speed up so the driver can't get in front of you
Adjust your speed to help leave a gap for the driver to merge
Close the gap to the car ahead
Stop in your lane until the driver merges
explanation: Cooperate with merging drivers. Racing to block them creates conflicts and can cause sideswipes and rear-end crashes.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., CO p. 22, CA p. 20, PA p. 50)

prompt: Where should you avoid changing lanes?
choices: On a straight road
In the middle of an intersection
On a road with broken white lane lines
On a road with more than two lanes
explanation: Make lane changes before or after an intersection, not in it. Vehicles and pedestrians in the intersection may not expect you.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., CA p. 21, NE p. 63, NJ p. 98)

prompt: You realize at the last second that you are in the wrong lane for your turn. What should you do?
choices: Cut across the other lanes to make the turn
Stop in your lane until you can merge over
Back up to the correct lane
Continue in your lane and find a safe place to turn around later
explanation: Last-minute lane changes cause crashes. If you miss a turn, keep going and safely and legally turn around.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., CA p. 21, NE p. 63, NJ p. 98)

prompt: On an undivided road with two lanes in each direction, how should you pass a slow vehicle in the right lane?
choices: Use the left lane on your side of the center line
Cross the center line into the oncoming lanes
Use the right shoulder
Use the center left-turn lane
explanation: When there are two or more lanes going your way, pass using those lanes. Do not drive left of the center line to pass.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., TX p. 37, NJ p. 67, AZ p. 32-33)

prompt: How should you position your car while driving in a lane?
choices: Over the left lane line so faster cars see you
Over the right edge line for extra space
Centered in the lane, without straddling the lane lines
Half in each lane to keep options open
explanation: Stay centered in your lane. Straddling lines confuses other drivers and blocks two lanes.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., CA p. 21, NE p. 63, NJ p. 98)

prompt: On a two-lane road you are driving well below the speed of traffic and a line of vehicles has built up behind you. What should you do?
choices: Keep going at your speed; it's their job to pass
Speed up well past the speed limit
Pull over where it is safe, such as a turnout, and let them pass
Drive partly on the shoulder without stopping
explanation: A slow driver holding up traffic should use a turnout or another safe spot to let vehicles by. This reduces risky passing.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., TX p. 37, NJ p. 67, AZ p. 32-33)

prompt: On a two-lane road the center line is broken on your side, but a curve ahead blocks your view. A slow car is in front of you. What should you do?
choices: Wait to pass until you can see far enough ahead
Pass now, because the broken line allows it
Pass and sound your horn through the curve
Pass on the right instead
explanation: A broken line means passing may be allowed, not that it is safe. Treat a curve or hill as if a car is coming just out of sight.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., AZ p. 28, PA p. 51, TX p. 44, NJ p. 67)

prompt: On a two-lane road, an oncoming car far ahead seems to be barely moving. What should you keep in mind before passing?
choices: A car that seems still is probably parked
You have plenty of time if you can't see it moving
Oncoming cars must slow down for you
It may be much closer and faster than it looks, so if in doubt, don't pass
explanation: Far-off oncoming vehicles often seem to be standing still. If you can clearly see it getting closer, it may already be too close to pass.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., MT p. 77, PA p. 51)

prompt: You start to pass on a two-lane road, but the car you're passing speeds up and an oncoming car appears. What is the safest action?
choices: Speed up as much as needed to finish the pass
Slow down and pull back into your lane behind the car
Stay beside the car and flash your lights
Move onto the left shoulder
explanation: If a pass is no longer safe, abort it: ease off, drop back and return to your lane. Do not count on other drivers to make room.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., CA p. 31, AZ p. 27, NY p. 39)

prompt: On a road with three lanes going your way, you are in the right lane and want to move to the center lane. What else should you look for besides traffic behind you?
choices: Pedestrians on the far sidewalk
A driver in the far-left lane who may also be moving into the center lane
Cars parked on the right
Your speedometer reading
explanation: Two drivers can try to enter the same lane at once from opposite sides. Check the lane beyond the one you are entering.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., CA p. 21, NE p. 63, NJ p. 98)

prompt: At an intersection, the car ahead of you stops to turn left and you pass it on the right. What extra hazards must you watch for?
choices: Cars behind you that may also turn left
Signs for upcoming exits
Nothing; the stopped car protects you
Oncoming cars turning left into your path and pedestrians or cyclists on the right
explanation: When passing on the right at an intersection, the stopped car blocks your view. Watch for oncoming left-turners and for people at the right side of the road.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., CA p. 31, NY p. 39-40, NJ p. 67, AZ p. 27)

prompt: On a two-lane road you want to pass two slow cars that are close together. When is that acceptable?
choices: Only if you can see a large enough gap ahead of the first car and enough clear road to finish safely
Any time, as long as you signal
Only if the second car moves onto the shoulder
Only if you pass one car on each side
explanation: Passing several vehicles takes much more time and space. Only do it if there is room to return in front of the lead vehicle and plenty of clear road.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., CA p. 31, AZ p. 27, NY p. 39)

prompt: Your mirrors are adjusted correctly. Do you still need to look over your shoulder before changing lanes?
choices: No, properly adjusted mirrors remove all blind spots
Only when changing lanes to the right
Yes, because even well-adjusted mirrors leave blind spots
Only when driving a large vehicle
explanation: Good mirror adjustment reduces blind spots but never eliminates them. Always glance over your shoulder before moving over.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., AZ p. 26, NY p. 39, NJ p. 98)

prompt: Why is speeding up while another vehicle is passing you on a two-lane road so dangerous?
choices: It is only a problem if you are already speeding
It makes your car use more fuel
The passing driver can get stuck in the oncoming lane, risking a head-on crash
It causes the other car to get a flat tire
explanation: If you speed up, the passing driver may not be able to get back in front of you before oncoming traffic arrives. Never increase speed when being passed.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., TX p. 45, AZ p. 27, NH p. 23)

prompt: A car ahead on a two-lane road stops to turn left. The only space to its right is an unpaved dirt shoulder. What is the safest choice?
choices: Wait behind the car until it turns
Drive onto the dirt shoulder to get around it
Pass it on the left
Honk until it moves
explanation: You may pass a left-turning car on the right only when there is room on the road to do it safely. Driving onto an unpaved shoulder is dangerous, so wait.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., CA p. 31, NY p. 39-40, NJ p. 67, AZ p. 27)

prompt: To pass a slow car on a two-lane road, you would have to go far over the speed limit. What should you do?
choices: Pass quickly, since a short burst of speed is safe
Pass, as long as you return to the speed limit afterward
Flash your lights until the driver speeds up
Don't pass; stay a safe distance behind
explanation: Pass only when you can do it safely without speeding. If the pass would take too much speed, it is not worth the risk.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., CA p. 31, AZ p. 27, NY p. 39)

prompt: Which situation makes passing on a two-lane road unsafe even when the center line is broken on your side?
choices: The car ahead is going slightly under the speed limit
Your view ahead is blocked or oncoming traffic is too close to complete the pass
It is a clear, sunny day
The road is straight and level
explanation: Markings only tell you where passing may be allowed. You must also have a clear view and enough space to return before meeting oncoming traffic.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., AZ p. 28, PA p. 51, TX p. 44, NJ p. 67)

prompt: You will be on a multilane highway for many miles and don't plan to pass anyone. Which lane choice is best?
choices: Use the far-left lane because it has fewer cars entering
Stay out of the far-left lane so it remains free for passing
Use the shoulder when traffic is light
Switch lanes often to keep a steady speed
explanation: Keep right except to pass. Using the left lane for steady cruising holds up passing traffic and leads to unsafe passing on the right.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., TX p. 37, NJ p. 67, AZ p. 32-33)

prompt: Traffic is heavy and slow where two lanes narrow to one. A driver stays in the ending lane until near the merge point and then takes a turn merging in. How should drivers in the open lane respond?
choices: Block the driver, since they should have merged earlier
Honk and close the gap
Move onto the shoulder to let the driver by
Let the driver merge in turn, alternating one car from each lane

prompt: You signal and check your mirror to change lanes, but during the head check you see a car in your blind spot. What should you do?
